accepted.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes ‘procedure established by law’ from ‘due process of law’ in the context of Article 21?
o: The former examines the fairness of law, whereas the latter examines only legislative enactment
The former requires a procedure enacted by the legislature, whereas the latter also examines whether the procedure is fair and reasonable
The former applies only to preventive detention, whereas the latter applies only to civil rights
Both expressions have exactly the same meaning in Indian constitutional law
accepted.x: ‘Procedure established by law’ requires compliance with a law enacted by the legislature. ‘Due process of law’ additionally requires the law and procedure to satisfy standards of fairness and reasonableness.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between two closely related constitutional expressions by identifying the additional fairness test.
accepted.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the A.K. Gopalan case:
1. It was decided in 1950.
2. It held that Article 21 protected an individual only against executive action.
3. It accepted that courts could examine the reasonableness of every law affecting personal liberty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: The A.K. Gopalan decision was delivered in 1950 and treated Article 21 as protection mainly against executive action. It did not permit courts to examine the reasonableness of the law in the later Maneka Gandhi sense.
accepted.tq: Find the statement that reverses the limited approach adopted in the earlier case.
accepted.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)?
o: Article 21 was confined exclusively to executive action
The Court rejected all elements of due process from Article 21
The procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable
Articles 14, 19 and 21 were treated as completely independent of one another
accepted.x: The Maneka Gandhi decision held that a procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable and must not be arbitrary.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise judicial test introduced by the later landmark judgment.
accepted.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

accepted.s: The expression ‘golden triangle’ of fundamental rights refers to the interrelationship among which Articles?
o: Articles 25, 26 and 29
Articles 14, 19 and 21
Articles 20, 21 and 22
Articles 15, 16 and 17
accepted.x: Maneka Gandhi established a close relationship among Articles 14, 19 and 21, commonly described as the golden triangle of fundamental rights.
accepted.tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping associated with the Maneka Gandhi doctrine.
accepted.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

accepted.s: Which one of the following is a major difference between the A.K. Gopalan and Maneka Gandhi approaches to Article 21?
o: A.K. Gopalan introduced American due process, whereas Maneka Gandhi restored the Japanese approach
A.K. Gopalan excluded legislative action from scrutiny under Article 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislation
A.K. Gopalan linked Articles 14, 19 and 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi separated them
A.K. Gopalan dealt with preventive detention, whereas Maneka Gandhi dealt only with property rights
accepted.x: A.K. Gopalan treated Article 21 narrowly and did not subject legislation to the later fairness review. Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against arbitrary legislative action.
accepted.tq: Compare the two cases across the exact dimensions of legislative scrutiny and Article 21 protection.
accepted.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

accepted.s:
Under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2), a person subjected to an ordinary arrest has which of the following rights?
1. To be informed of the grounds of arrest
2. To consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice
3. To be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding journey time
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Article 22(1) and 22(2) provide all three safeguards in the case of an ordinary arrest: information about the grounds, legal representation, and production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.
accepted.tq: Check the complete constitutional package of safeguards rather than selecting only one arrest right.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: The safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2) are not available to which of the following persons under Article 22(3)?
o: A person produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
An enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law
A person arrested under an ordinary warrant
Every person arrested for a criminal offence
accepted.x: Article 22(3) excludes an enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law from the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2).
accepted.tq: Use the constitutional exceptions to ordinary-arrest safeguards as the decisive pair.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2)?
o: Deportation of an alien
Arrest under a court order
Civil arrest
All of the above
accepted.x: The listed situations—arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens—are not covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and 22(2).
accepted.tq: Test the scope of an exception by identifying all situations excluded from the ordinary-arrest guarantee.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which provisions correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC provisions concerning communication of grounds of arrest and production before a magistrate?
o: Sections 47 and 58; earlier Sections 50 and 57 of the CrPC
Sections 50 and 57; earlier Sections 47 and 58 of the CrPC
Sections 22 and 24; earlier Sections 20 and 21 of the CrPC
Sections 58 and 60; earlier Sections 47 and 50 of the CrPC
accepted.x: Sections 47 and 58 of the BNSS correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC Sections 50 and 57 concerning the relevant arrest safeguards.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between present BNSS section numbers and their earlier CrPC counterparts.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes preventive detention?
o: Detention based on suspicion of future acts and imposed without a criminal trial
Detention exclusively for non-payment of a civil debt
Detention after conviction for the purpose of executing a sentence
Detention ordered only by a criminal court after a finding of guilt
accepted.x: Preventive detention is detention without trial based on the apprehension that a person may commit specified harmful acts in the future. Punitive detention follows conviction.
accepted.tq: Separate preventive detention from punitive detention by focusing on timing and purpose.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: A person detained under a preventive detention law may ordinarily be detained beyond three months only when:
o: An Advisory Board reports sufficient cause for continued detention
The President personally reviews the detention
The detainee waives the right of representation
The police commissioner grants written permission
accepted.x: Article 22(4) requires an Advisory Board, consisting of High Court judges or persons qualified to be High Court judges, to report sufficient cause before preventive detention continues beyond three months.
accepted.tq: Ask which constitutional authority supplies the mandatory safeguard for extended preventive detention.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention under Article 22:
1. The grounds of detention must be communicated to the detainee.
2. The detainee must be given the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order.
3. Parliament may prescribe the maximum period for which a person may be detained under a preventive detention law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Article 22(5) requires communication of grounds and the earliest opportunity for representation. Article 22(7) permits Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention in the circumstances specified by the Constitution.
accepted.tq: Combine safeguards under Article 22(5) with Parliament’s power under Article 22(7).
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 reduced the constitutional period for preventive detention without an Advisory Board report from three months to:
o: One month
Four months
Six months
Two months
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment reduced the period from three months to two months. However, the relevant provision has not been notified, so the three-month period continues to operate.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the amended constitutional text from the provision that is actually in force.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Why does the three-month period continue to apply to preventive detention despite the 44th Amendment?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the two-month provision
Article 22 does not contain any period relating to an Advisory Board
Parliament repealed the entire 44th Amendment
The amended provision was never notified
accepted.x: Although the 44th Amendment substituted two months for three months, the relevant amended clause has never been notified. Consequently, the three-month rule continues to apply.
accepted.tq: Use the implementation-status trap: distinguish an enacted amendment from a notified and operative provision.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Which subject–legislative competence pair is correctly matched in relation to preventive detention?
o: Defence, foreign affairs and security of India — Parliament alone; public order and security of a State — Parliament and the States
Defence and foreign affairs — States alone; public order — Parliament alone
Public order — Parliament alone; security of India — States alone
Supplies essential to the community — States alone in every circumstance
accepted.x: Parliament alone legislates on preventive detention connected with defence, foreign affairs and the security of India. Parliament and the States may legislate on public order, security of a State and supplies essential to the community.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure exclusive Union subjects and then match the concurrent preventive-detention subjects.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to which of the following?
o: Mere law and order in every local dispute
Any administrative inconvenience caused by an individual
Public order, but not merely routine law and order
Only a civil disagreement between private parties
accepted.x: The Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order. Preventive detention cannot be justified merely by routine law-and-order concerns.
accepted.tq: Use the higher-threshold comparison between public order and ordinary law and order.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s:
Arrange the following preventive detention laws in chronological order of enactment:
A. National Security Act
B. Maintenance of Internal Security Act
C. Preventive Detention Act
D. Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act
o: C, B, D, A
B, C, D, A
C, D, B, A
D, C, B, A
accepted.x: The Preventive Detention Act was enacted in 1950, MISA in 1971, COFEPOSA in 1974 and the National Security Act in 1980.
accepted.tq: Place the laws by their enactment years, using the earliest and latest items first.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: NSA, 1980 — State law applicable only in Kerala
Preventive Detention Act, 1950 — First preventive detention law; lapsed in 1969
MISA, 1971 — Repealed in 1969
COFEPOSA, 1974 — Anti-terror and unlawful-associations law
accepted.x: The Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was the first such law and lapsed in 1969. MISA was repealed in 1978, COFEPOSA concerns smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders, and NSA is a central law.
accepted.tq: Find the correctly matched law by checking both its date and its distinctive legal purpose or status.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 is associated with which of the following?
o: Detention of foreign-exchange offenders and repeal in 1969
Its use during the Emergency and repeal in 1978
A state preventive detention law operating only in Jammu and Kashmir
A law enacted in 1980 for detention up to twelve months
accepted.x: MISA was enacted in 1971, used during the Emergency and repealed in 1978.
accepted.tq: Link the statute with its distinctive historical context and repeal year.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: Which preventive detention law is specifically associated with suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators?
o: MISA, 1971
COFEPOSA, 1974
UAPA, 1967
accepted.x: The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, or COFEPOSA, targets suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders.
accepted.tq: Use the subject-matter clue in the statute’s title to identify the correct law.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: Which of the following statements about the National Security Act, 1980 is correct?
o: It permits detention up to twelve months without charges
It is a state law applicable only to Kerala
It was repealed in 1978 after the Emergency
It was the first preventive detention law and lapsed in 1969
accepted.x: The National Security Act, 1980 permits preventive detention for up to twelve months without charges, subject to constitutional and statutory safeguards.
accepted.tq: Match the statute with its distinctive maximum detention period rather than its general name.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with UAPA?
o: UAPA, 1967 — Anti-terror and unlawful-associations law
UAPA, 1967 — Kerala’s state preventive detention law
UAPA, 1967 — Law exclusively concerning foreign exchange
UAPA, 1967 — First preventive detention law, lapsed in 1969
accepted.x: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 is associated with terrorism and unlawful associations. The other descriptions relate to different laws.
accepted.tq: Avoid the law-name swap by matching UAPA with its stated anti-terror and unlawful-associations role.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs consists entirely of State preventive detention laws?
o: J&K PSA and Kerala KAPA
NSA and COFEPOSA
MISA and UAPA
Preventive Detention Act and NSA
accepted.x: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act and the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act are state-level preventive detention laws. NSA, COFEPOSA, MISA, UAPA and the Preventive Detention Act are central enactments.
accepted.tq: Classify laws by territorial level and eliminate central statutes from the state-law pair.
accepted.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

accepted.s: The historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India are associated with which pair?
o: The Charter Act of 1813 and the Indian Councils Act of 1909
Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act
The Government of India Act, 1935 and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951
accepted.x: Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act are identified as important historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India.
accepted.tq: Recall the historically paired antecedents instead of later constitutional or electoral enactments.
accepted.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

accepted.s: Which constitutional change was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 in relation to Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency?
o: It made both Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable during every Emergency
It transferred the power under Article 359 from the President to the Supreme Court
It removed Article 21 from the list of Fundamental Rights
It ensured that an order under Article 359 could not suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment inserted the protection that the right to move courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359, even during a National Emergency.
accepted.tq: Identify the amendment’s protective effect and reject the reversal that makes Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable.
accepted.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable during a National Emergency.
2. The protection relating to Articles 20 and 21 was inserted into Article 359 by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
3. The President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of every Fundamental Right during an Emergency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 359 does not permit suspension of the right to enforce Articles 20 and 21; its operation concerns other Fundamental Rights subject to constitutional limits.
accepted.tq: Spot the overbroad word ‘every’ in the statement about the President’s Article 359 power.
accepted.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

accepted.s: The 44th Amendment’s protection of Articles 20 and 21 was principally a constitutional response to which development?
o: The ADM Jabalpur judgment of 1976
The Minerva Mills judgment of 1980
The Kesavananda Bharati judgment of 1973
The S.R. Bommai judgment of 1994
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment responded to the ADM Jabalpur decision of 1976, which had permitted suspension of the right to life and personal liberty during the Emergency.
accepted.tq: Link the corrective constitutional amendment with the earlier judicial decision it sought to address.
accepted.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

accepted.s: Which judgment overruled the approach of ADM Jabalpur concerning the right to life and personal liberty?
o: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Golaknath v. State of Punjab
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
accepted.x: The K.S. Puttaswamy judgment of 2017 overruled the approach taken in ADM Jabalpur concerning the suspension of Article 21 protections.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the later corrective privacy judgment from the earlier Article 21 cases.
accepted.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

accepted.s: Which additional change relating to a National Emergency was made by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978?
o: The ground of ‘internal disturbance’ under Article 352 was replaced by ‘armed rebellion’
The ground of ‘armed rebellion’ under Article 352 was replaced by ‘internal disturbance’
Article 352 was repealed entirely
The power to proclaim an Emergency was transferred exclusively to the Supreme Court
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment replaced ‘internal disturbance’ with the more specific expression ‘armed rebellion’ as a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352.
accepted.tq: Test the direction of the constitutional wording change by separating the old and new expressions.
accepted.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act
